No, the hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken; we gave a fair proportion of our literature to the eastern pip-vinces. Remember I am an eastern province man myself, and if I had not been actuated by a stern sense of duty to give every place a fair show, I would want to talk-as much as possible about Quebec. But 1 did not allow any special representation of that province at Liege, because I wanted to keep the national characteristic of the exhibit and not have special representatives of the provinces or special exhibits of provinces separately. We take our exhibits from every part of the Dominion, giving the name of the locality, and, where we get it from a private party, the name of the party. But, at the same time, it is a homogeneous Canadian national exhibit.

The minister said he was negotiating with some gentlemen from Alanitoba to go as representatives to this

exhibition. It is high time that gentleman was despatched. If the minister will tell ns who it is he is negotiating with, we from the province of Manitoba may be able to tell him if he is the best man.
I do not wish to use the gentleman's name .before the matter is settled, but, if he accepts, my bon. friend (Mr. Staples) will recognize that he is the best man for this service.
I did not get the names of the representatives of the several provinces.
I have given the list a couple of times already. I can go over it again, if the hon. gentleman desires.
What expert knowledge had Mr. Tolmie?
He has gone as accountant, to take charge of the book-keeping and accounts. He has been seven or eight years in banking and has been in charge of a branch bank. He is a thoroughly competent man.
What is his age?
Twenty-six or twenty-seven, I think.
I understand he is 22.
I think the hon. gentleman must be mistaken.
What bank was he manager of?
He was in charge of one of the branches of the Merchants Bank at some place in Ontario.
Is he a son of the member?
Yes.
What is Mr. Turriff's occupation?
I think he is a farmer.
An expert on exhibitions?
No, these gentlemen are appointed on this special exhibition, in addition to the regular staff whose names I have given.
Are you sending any one from Alberta?
No.
Why is Alberta not represented?
You can't have every place represented unless you enlarge the staff.

Looking over the Auditor General's Report, there seems to be a certain amount of. looseness in these accounts. We find that the Auditor General finds fault with the way in which things are
managed. He speaks of some accounts four years old and not settled, of large amounts of money paid and no accounts of disbursements. Now, I think it is all right to spend money on these exhibitions, and to pay men fair salaries for their work in connection with it, but in many of these cases you find funds unaccounted for-some $400, some $1,000, and so on. And this in the case of men receiving as much as $9,000 a year or $6,000 or $4,000.
Which of them received $9,000?
Mr. Hutchison.
That is one man. Is there any other?
I said one man. Will the hon. gentlemen tell me what Mr. Burns receives?
He receives $1,700 a year and payment for what travelling he does in Canada.
Last year, lie received $3,770 in addition.
Where does the hon. gentleman find that?
At page D-26 of the Auditor General's Report.
That was when Mr. Burns was in New Zealand.
It is in the last report we have.
Mr. Burns was sent to New Zealand a year ago last winter, and while engaged in that trip he received his ordinary salary and $10 a day for living allowance.
So I was correct in the statement I made. Now, I want to ask the minister with reference to one or two of the men in his employ. What are the duties of A. L. Jarvis?
He is secretary of the department.
What were his duties in going from Ottawa to Victoria, as appear on the same page, 26 ?
Mr. Jarvis went out to Victoria to see about a shipment of goods from Canada to New Zealand.
Was it necessary for him to take a large amount of baggage with him during that trip, which lasted a month ?
I do not know that he did.
Were any of Mr. Jarvis's accounts disputed in the Auditor General's Department ?

I cannot say offhand. I * understand that when he went to Victoria

he took his wife with him, and by error the drawing room which he took was charged to him. Immediately on his return, when he found it had been charged to him, he went to the Auditor General and refunded, stating that it had been improperly charged.
That would not appear in the Auditor General's Report. Do members of the minister's department pay full fare on the railways the same as ordinary travellers ?
Mr. Jarvis does.
How is it that in this account all that is entered up for his first trip from Ottawa to Vancouver and return, is $101.65 ?
I cannot say.
We find that for tlie next trip he makes to Vancouver, he charges $131. Now one of these must be wrong.
My deputy informs me that the rates vary with the season. One rate is for the winter and the other is for the summer.
Would the minister think it was an unusual rate to pay $67 for 6 days board at a hotel in Vancouver ?
Is that in the Auditor General's Report ?

I get this from a return. We find in this return that there is a drawing room from Ottawa to Winnipeg, $30 ; from Winnipeg to Victoria, $30 ; from Victoria to Ottawa, $35. We find that is refunded. I understand from the minister that this man had nothing to do outside of going to the coast. Was It necessary for him to make any disbursements except on his crwn account ?
I cannot say.
Does that man's duty require him to make any disbursements except on account of his own living expenses ?
It is quite possible. I have not the accounts before me. He may have had to make some petty disbursements on account of the department. But what is the hon. gentleman reading from ?

Go all through these accounts and you will find that kind of thing existing. The Minister of Agriculture spoke a while ago with regard to Mr. Despard. Has there been any objection to any of his accounts, either in the hon. gentleman's department or in the Auditor General's Department ?

As to the Mr. Jarvis' expense account which the hon. gentleman has just read, all the items have been passed both in my department and in the Auditor General's Department, aud apparently have been approved. I think it is sufficient. I never knew anything about them until now. As to the gentleman last named, there has been no protest from the Auditor General that I am aware of. But I was informed that Mr. Jarvis found certain payments charged to him in the accounts of the department which he knew were not properly charged to him, and he went aud made a refund, owing to having had his wife with him. I know of no other protest from the Auditor General with regard to this man.
Has there been any exception taken to Mr. Despard's accounts with the department?
Not that I am aware of.
Is there more than one Despard in the employ of the government.
Not that I have heard of.
I understand that Despard received $100 a month. We find that he receives $75 and that another Despard receives $25. I would like some information as to this.

I understand that while Mr. Despard was away in New Zealand his mother was to receive a certain payment, that she was paid one month $25 and that by mistake he was also paid $25 in New Zealand. On his return his account was looked into and he returned the $25 which had been paid to his mother.
Is it not a fact that your department paid the ocean fares of some men employed in connection with these exhibitions which money has not been refunded ?
I am informed by my officers that they do not know of any such thing having taken place.
The returns show where the government has paid the Canadian Pacific Railway for the passage of some of these men's wives from San Francisco to Auckland and that this has to be refunded.
I am informed that they did not go by the Canadian Pacific Railway in the first place and I am satisfied that the fare of nobody's wife was paid by the department.
Well, the reports belie your statement.
What reports?
Your own reports that are before the Public Accounts Committee.

Does my hon. friend say that the reports before the Public Accounts Committee show that the Department of Agriculture paid the fares of the wives of some of these officers going to New Zealand and that the money was not refunded ?

I say that the returns show that the return fares of some of these men and their wives were paid from San Francisco to Auckland and that they were to be refunded to this government.
Ml*. FISHER. If my hon. friend can show me that I will have it investigated. I think my hon. friend mpst be in error.
I am certainly not in error.

Then I will investigate the matter and I am satisfied that we will find that if any such payment was made it was repaid by the husband. It may be possible that a ticket was taken for his wife at the same time that the department 337
secured a ticket for him. It is the practice of the department to purchase tickets for officers who are sent to these different exhibitions. It may be that some officer asked that a ticket be taken for his wife at the same time his ticket was taken for him and that it was charged up against his salary or other payment. I do not know whether that is the case or not, but I will have it investigated. I will say that if any such payment was made the individual on whose behalf it was made had to refund it and did refund it, and that the department is not out of pocket for the passage money of anybody's wife.
This return shows it has not been refunded and that it has to be refunded ; $750 is the fare of two from San Francisco to Auckland and return.
What is the name?
I do not purpose mentioning the name.
I would like the hon. gentleman to state the name of the individual.

I do not purpose mentioning the name of any one. Some of the best citizens of Canada who have gone to foreign countries representing manufacturing concerns do not speak very highly of the deportment of some of the officials sent out by the Minister of Agriculture to represent Canada at these exhibitions. I suppose the minister would like me to name my authority, but I do not propose to do it. One of the most prominent Canadians living to-day outside of Canada said that the deportment of these officials was not creditable to Canada.
If the hon. gentleman does not wish to give the names publicly, let him give me them privately, and if any of my officers have been guilty of such conduct I will dismiss them from the service.
I do not object to $10 a day for living expenses, but I do object to $10 a day for living expenses when it goes in booze.
If my hon. friend will give me the names of any of my officers who have been guilty of misconduct I will inquire into the matter.
It is the duty of the department to send out representatives who will uphold the dignity of Canada.
Certainly.

For Heaven's sake cut out that tag end to every man's account, 'other expenses not accounted for.' It would be well for the department to consider the character of the men who go on these excursions and see that they conduct themselves the way they should. I do not expect that the Minister of Agriculture will



appoint Conservatives, but I expect him to appoint good Liberals. There are plenty of good Liberals in the country who will represent Canada as she should be represented. It does seem to me that in every department it is almost impossible to prevent crookedness and irregularities. The men who have the patronage seem to have a pull with the heads of departments, and they recommend men who are not qualified to fill public positions. That is the case throughout the length and breadth of the country. Fully 25 per cent of the expenditures noted in the Auditor General's Report is practically thrown to the winds and it brings disgrace and discredit to Canada.

It is our duty to appoint men who will be a credit to the country, and I believe I have done so. If the hon. gentleman gives me the names privately of any men who have misconducted themselves I shall investigate, and if any one of them is guilty he shall have short shrift so far as my department is concerned.

The minister has a good deal of information to bring down with regard to this item, and as it is now time to conclude the work of the day, the item can pass and the information can be brought down later.
I wish to discuss the matter of home exhibitions, and if that can be done on some other item, I have no objection that this should pass.

If my hon. friend refers to the Dominion grant for the Canadian exhibition he can discuss that on the item for that purpose.
Imperial Institute, $6,000.
How much was spent last year?

Practically the whole of it. We contribute $2,500 to the institute, and in return the authorities keep our exhibits in order. We pay $1,500 to Mr. Harrison Watson, curator of the museum ; $500 for office assistance, rental towards the city office of the Institute $1,225, and the balance in adding to the exhibit and for incidental expenses.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.

Before the House adjourns, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance a question with regard to the return brought down by the Prime Minister containing correspondence with the moral and social reform council of Canada. One of the letters refers to another letter of April 20. and that letter is not on the file.
Will the hon. Minister of Finance draw the Prime Minister's attention to it and have this missing letter brought down?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a return brought down by the Prime Minister, and I am sure he will take notice of my hon. friend's remarks.
What will we take up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Several Bills on the Order Paper, beginning with the Act to amend the Railway Act, with respect to telegraphs and telephones; second reading of Bill to amend the Post Office Act; Bill respecting reformatories in Nova Scotia; Bill respecting the use otf tobacco by young persons, and afterwards Supply with the items of the Agriculture Department.
